title: What cameras can learn about hand movements
lead: Grounded Superintelligence and BitRobot used cameras worn on the head to record 10,000 hours of work. Seeing the same action from several angles helps them locate the hand as it handles an object.

news.title: What six cameras see when people work with their hands
news.summary: Grounded Superintelligence and BitRobot used wearable cameras to record people doing physical work. The different viewpoints help locate the hands in space and preserve their movements as examples for robot learning.
news.details: Grounded Superintelligence and BitRobot collected 10,000 hours of recordings of human work in 11 countries.
news.technical_novelty: A headset with six synchronized cameras and inertial sensors supports three-dimensional estimates of head and hand movement.
news.engineering_impact: The recordings provide examples of physical tasks for teams developing robot learning systems.
news.limitations: The data contain no force or touch measurements. The paper does not evaluate training on a robot.
news.evidence_status: The authors describe the dataset, hardware and processing in a preprint.
news.body:
Grounded Superintelligence and BitRobot filmed people handling objects by mounting several cameras on a headset. The goal was to collect examples for robot learning and recover where the hands were at each point in a task. An object can hide part of the hand from one viewpoint, so having another angle can give the software information that a single recording would miss.

The 250-gram headset carries six synchronized cameras and two inertial measurement units that measure acceleration and rotation. The cameras view the wearer's hands from different angles. The processing combines the views and sensor readings to estimate head motion and three-dimensional hand positions. Each recording session has its own calibration, which lets the processing account for the positions and characteristics of the cameras.

The authors selected 10,000 hours of elapsed recording time. A minute filmed by several cameras counts as one minute. They segmented recordings from 11 countries into 1,378,462 clips with a median duration of 17.8 seconds. The authors say participants gave written consent and were compensated for taking part. Audio is excluded and faces are obscured.

On film you can tell the direction in which a worker moved a hand and when they reached for the next object. Some parts of the task are harder to see. If a person wipes a beaker, finger positions give clues about how they held the paper towel, but the team did not measure how hard they pressed on the glass. The paper describes what was captured and leaves the question of what a robot can learn from it for another study.

news.title: Did the robot pick the thing it was asked for?
news.summary: Researchers at the University of Science and Technology of China and their partners tested robot controllers in virtual scenes. They kept the arrangement of objects the same and changed the request to see whether the arm would pick a different target when asked.
news.details: The test suite contains 48 held-out simulation scenes. In ten target-selection scenes, the team changed instructions while keeping the starting arrangement fixed.
news.technical_novelty: ManipScope tests whether a robot controller changes its action when the instruction names a different object or destination.
news.engineering_impact: The results help isolate errors in selecting a target before assessing execution of the chosen movement.
news.limitations: The study ran in simulation and withheld demonstrations for the held-out scenes.
news.evidence_status: The researchers reported their results and control runs in a preprint.
news.organization: University of Science and Technology of China, Sharpa Robotics, Shanghai Jiao Tong University and The Chinese University of Hong Kong
news.body:
A research team led by the University of Science and Technology of China asked a question that is easy to overlook when watching a robot demo. If the instructions name another object on the same table, will the arm change what it reaches for? To find out, the researchers built a virtual test called ManipScope, which lets them reset the table to the same layout after every attempt.

The team organized the tasks into six families and withheld demonstrations for the 48 evaluation scenes. To test the role of the instruction, it reused starting arrangements and varied the command in ten target-selection scenes. A single successful attempt can happen if a model picks the object that tends to appear in a familiar location. A series of instructions tests whether the same model can take the correct action for each command from an identical starting state.

Pooling the results of ten saved model versions, the team reported that all instructions were followed in 39 of 1,000 states, or 3.9%. A control that received no instruction text scored 16% on that measure. In a separate analysis of 12 model versions across 13,200 runs in 11 scenes, 84.6% of failed attempts involved moving a distractor, an object that was present but was not the intended target. The two figures count different things: one counts complete sets of instructions and the other describes how individual attempts failed.

Picking a target and handling it are two separate skills. An arm can lift an object neatly and carry it to the right place while still making a mistake about which item was wanted. That is why the researchers looked for those slips separately. Their virtual table can be restored exactly between attempts, while a physical trial would also have to deal with objects shifting and differences in how the gripper makes contact.

news.title: How a fleet of robots shares a narrow aisle
news.summary: OMRON Robotics opened orders in the Americas and Europe for two robots that move loads inside buildings. Each finds its way using nearby features, while shared software assigns jobs and coordinates routes.
news.details: OMRON Robotics opened orders for two indoor carriers rated for 150 and 300 kilograms.
news.technical_novelty: The carriers navigate using their surroundings without floor markers, while fleet software assigns transport jobs.
news.engineering_impact: A site trial can establish how room to manoeuvre, charging and traffic in both directions affect the amount moved per shift.
news.limitations: The published figures are product specifications. The company expects shipments to start in January 2027.
news.evidence_status: The source is the manufacturer, whose announcement gives no throughput measurements from a customer site.
news.body:
OMRON Robotics has begun taking orders for two mobile carriers that move loads indoors. The carriers are narrow enough for a one-metre aisle. Each vehicle uses features in its surroundings to work out its position, but several vehicles in the same building also need a way to share the routes between pickup and drop-off points.

The smaller LD-150 is rated to carry 150 kg and is 500 mm wide. For the LD-300 the corresponding figures are 300 kg and 580 mm. OMRON specifies operation in aisles as narrow as one metre, a series top speed of 2.1 m/s and the ability to handle a slope of up to five degrees. The vehicles estimate their position using features in their surroundings and do not require guide tape or floor markers.

OMRON's FLOW Core software assigns jobs, plans routes and coordinates the movements of the fleet. The vendor says it can manage up to 100 compatible OMRON vehicles of different types. Inductive charging transfers power at a station without a plug and can take as little as 18 minutes according to the company. Orders opened in the Americas and Europe, with other regions to follow. The vendor expects shipments to begin in January 2027.

Finding your position and deciding which trip to make are different jobs. A vehicle needs a sense of where it is next to the racks, while fleet software can assign jobs across the group and coordinate routes that share an aisle. One figure the announcement leaves open is how long the robots wait for one another when several loaded trips converge. Measuring that delay would show how much extra work a larger fleet can actually do in an existing building.

news.title: How a wiring diagram becomes a physical assembly plan
news.summary: Munich startup Vetaion raised €5.7 million to develop machinery and software for assembling control cabinets. Its software converts flat electrical drawings into spatial layouts intended to tell a robot where the components belong.
news.details: Munich startup Vetaion raised €5.7 million to develop equipment and software for industrial control cabinet assembly.
news.technical_novelty: Its software converts two-dimensional electrical plans into a three-dimensional layout of cabinet components.
news.engineering_impact: Vetaion intends to use the digital layout to develop automated component placement and wiring.
news.limitations: The public announcements provide no verified measurements from customer factories.
news.evidence_status: Investor UVC Partners and entrepreneurship centre UnternehmerTUM announced the funding.
news.body:
Munich startup Vetaion has raised money to develop tools for assembling factory control cabinets, the boxes that hold parts which supply power and send control signals to machinery. The project tackles the step between seeing how the parts should be connected on a drawing and giving a machine enough information to put them into a real cabinet and wire them together.

Munich startup Vetaion raised €5.7 million in an early funding round. UVC Partners and Visionaries Tomorrow led the round, with 2100 Ventures and Viessmann Generations Group also taking part. UVC Partners and the Munich entrepreneurship centre UnternehmerTUM announced the financing.

Vetaion's software uses a flat electrical drawing to produce a three-dimensional layout of the parts. A wiring diagram shows which elements are connected, while a spatial layout gives them positions inside the cabinet. The team is developing equipment intended to use that layout to mount components and connect them with wires. The funding supports work on this combination of software and machinery.

Knowing which sockets should be connected still leaves a question about how to reach them. A component beside a socket can change the direction from which a tool can approach it. That is where a spatial layout becomes useful to an assembly machine. The announcements give no trial result that would establish how many different layouts the equipment has managed to assemble from start to finish.

news.title: Who is running NVIDIA after Huang’s return?
news.summary: NVIDIA says Jensen Huang is back in charge. Reuters confirmed the leadership change, while the separate internal inquiry described by the board continues.
news.details: The board reinstated Huang as president, chief executive and director. Colette Kress remains chief financial officer.
news.technical_novelty: A planned compliance chief complements the board’s national security and export control committee.
news.engineering_impact: A computing supplier used by robotics teams is changing how it oversees trade compliance.
news.limitations: The independent internal inquiry continues. The announcement gives no revised hardware delivery terms.
news.evidence_status: NVIDIA’s announcement, its filing with the US securities regulator and Reuters confirm the leadership decision.
news.body:
Jensen Huang is back in charge at NVIDIA, a company that makes processors used, among other things, to train programs that control robots. NVIDIA made the announcement on November 23. Huang regained the positions of president, chief executive and director. The board makes major decisions for the company, while the chief executive is responsible for running it day to day.

In its filing with the US securities regulator, NVIDIA dates the board action to November 22. The company made it public the following day, and Reuters independently reported Huang’s return. The directors voted unanimously. Colette Kress, who had been running the company on an interim basis, remains chief financial officer. Harvey Jones stays on as board chair.

The board said it had heard from senior US government officials and believes Huang’s return poses no national security risk. That is the board’s assessment. NVIDIA says it created a committee of independent directors after reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The committee and its outside counsel will continue the inquiry. NVIDIA also began looking for a company-wide compliance chief to oversee adherence to rules. Its board has a dedicated committee supervising national security and export control.

Picking a person to run the company today and finding out what happened during the period under review are different pieces of work. The independent directors and their lawyers are still investigating. NVIDIA’s announcement therefore identifies who has which job, while the inquiry has yet to produce its conclusion. The compliance chief the company is now seeking will report to the board committee responsible for nominations and corporate governance.

technology_signal.title: One training example from several viewpoints
technology_signal.summary: Grounded Superintelligence and BitRobot filmed people's hands from several angles at once. Images and sensor readings let them estimate how the head and hands moved through space.
technology_signal.implications: The recordings preserve sequences of movement that could be used to teach robots. They do not measure how much force a person applied to an object.
